analysis.one_liner: Bans unsafe handguns lacking child-safety features, tightens rules on gun dealers, and penalizes leaving guns accessible to kids.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required new handguns to have child-safety features such as devices that stop firing when the magazine is removed or that prevent a young child from pulling the trigger. It would have banned selling semiautomatic assault weapons to people under 18, taken away the federal license of a dealer who willfully sells a gun to a minor, required two forms of ID from buyers under 24, set safety standards for gun shops, and made it a crime to leave a loaded gun where a child can get it, with fines up to $10,000. It also funded school programs teaching children about gun dangers, state tracking of children's firearm injuries, and expansion of a program that traces guns used in youth crimes.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and their families gain the most: the bill targets the main paths by which children get shot—unsecured loaded guns at home, guns sold to minors, handguns that fire when dropped or that a child can operate, and assault weapons reaching teenagers. Schools and community groups gain grant funding for gun-violence prevention education, and state health and police agencies gain money to track and investigate children's firearm injuries [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children and families at risk of gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Makes it illegal to manufacture or import a handgun that fails a drop test, lacks a magazine disconnect safety, or can be discharged by an unauthorized user, with exemptions for child-resistant triggers requiring a 10-pound pull [S2] [S3].
Extends the existing ban on selling handguns to juveniles to semiautomatic assault weapons and doubles the prison term, to 20 years, for giving a juvenile a gun to use in a violent crime [S2] [S3].

Requires the Treasury to revoke the federal license of a dealer who willfully sells a firearm to someone under 18, requires two IDs from buyers under 24, and sets minimum safety and security standards for gun shops with inspections and penalties [S2] [S3].

Makes it a federal offense, punishable by up to $10,000 and a year in prison, to keep a loaded firearm within a child's reach without a locking device, with exceptions for law enforcement, self-defense, and lawful entry situations [S2] [S3].

Authorizes roughly $66 million a year combined for grants to schools for gun-violence prevention education, to state health and law enforcement agencies for tracking children's firearm injuries, and to cities for tracing guns used in youth crimes [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Gun manufacturers and importers would have to redesign or retrofit handguns to add safety mechanisms, and licensed dealers would bear the cost of shop security upgrades, extra record-checking, and the risk of losing their license. Taxpayers fund the grant programs, and individual gun owners face fines if a child accesses an unsecured loaded gun [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Mandated safety designs fall on manufacturers and dealers: drop-test compliance, magazine disconnect safeties, authorized-user mechanisms, and shop security standards would impose real compliance costs that could be passed to buyers [S2] [S3].

The child-access provision creates a federal penalty of up to $10,000 and one year in prison for gun owners who keep a loaded firearm where a child can reach it, a liability even careful owners could face if a child gains access unexpectedly, though it carves out exceptions for locked storage, law enforcement, self-defense, and break-ins [S2] [S3].

Design mandates raise the good-faith objection that mechanical requirements could add cost and complexity to firearms used for self-defense, though the bill includes exemptions for child-resistant triggers and does not ban any class of gun outright [S2] [S3].

The grant programs—about $60 million a year for school education, $5 million a year for injury surveillance, and $1.5 million for a safety study—add federal spending subject to annual appropriation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety provisions target narrow, well-defined harms—children firing unsecured guns, dealers selling to minors, assault weapons reaching teenagers—rather than restricting gun ownership broadly, and the bill preserves self-defense and law-enforcement exceptions. The main costs are compliance expenses for the firearms industry and modest federal spending, weighed against child deaths and injuries that unsecured guns cause each year. The strongest design critique is that the safe-storage penalty could ensnare otherwise careful owners, but the bill limits it with storage-device and other exceptions.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy, joined by Sens. Boxer, Durbin, and Schumer as original sponsors, introduced the Children's Gun Violence Prevention Act of 1999 on March 25, 1999 [S3] [S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].

No further action appears in the record: the committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and the full Senate never debated or voted on it before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1] [S5].
The bill drew six cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers, importers, and licensed dealers are better off because the bill died: they never faced the mandated safety designs, shop-security standards, two-ID requirement, or automatic license revocation. Families and communities concerned about children's access to guns gained nothing from its failure.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on [S4].

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (Republican-controlled)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill—no hearing, markup, or report—after the Senate referred it on March 25, 1999 [S5].

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As the committee chair who controlled its agenda, never scheduled action on the bill, which sat without a markup for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal gun-safety mandates, waiting-period expansions, and child-access penalties during this period, lobbying against similar 1999 gun-control measures.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Judiciary Committee never moved the bill, so support and inaction split along party lines.

industries.note: The bill would have barred them from making or importing handguns that fail a drop test, lack a magazine disconnect safety, or lack a device preventing discharge by an unauthorized user, forcing design changes industry has long resisted. These features directly address children firing guns they find or take.

Dealers would have faced automatic license revocation for willfully selling to minors, a two-ID requirement for buyers under 24, minimum shop security standards, annual inspections, and new penalties. Stricter dealer rules target the retail channel through which guns reach juveniles.

The bill added federal design mandates, dealer regulation, and a child-access crime with fines and prison time—the kinds of federal firearms regulation these groups oppose and lobbied against in this era.
